newsitem.title: MALTA: Arabs see Middle East as priority in talks with EU.
newsitem.headline: Arabs see Middle East as priority in talks with EU.

text.p: Israel and the Palestinians prepared for a showdown in Malta, where on Tuesday their delegations face each other at a meeting of European and Mediterranean foreign ministers.

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, the likely focus of Arab criticism, decided on Monday to attend, his ministry said. He had apparently hesitated to appear at a forum where the Arab delegations outnumber his team eight to one.

On the other side of the fence, Palestinian President Yasser Arafat will relish the opportunity to tell a largely sympathetic audience that Israel's settlement policy in East Jerusalem is the main reason peace talks have collapsed.
Palestinians have clashed with Israeli troops in the West Bank almost every day since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu started work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on March 18.
The Arabs say Netanyahu must go back on his decision, Israel says the issue is the violent response by Palestinians.

Europeans would like to keep the Middle East crisis in the background and concentrate on long-term economic and security ties between the northern and southern shores of the Mediterranean, diplomats say.
"We're worried the Middle East peace problems might hijack the agenda and overshadow all the good work the Europeans have been doing," one European diplomat said.
"All the rancour will be directed at Israel but Levy and Arafat will be side by side. In the present context, that's a remarkable result in itself," he added.
Palestinian spokesman Nabil Abu Rdainah said Levy and Arafat would not meet on Malta.
The Arabs, especially those in the eastern Mediterranean, argue that a debate on security cannot ignore Israel's attitude in the Middle East peace talks.

"The Arab concept is linked to developments in the Middle East peace process, because a bigger threat to security and stability comes from what is happening there," said Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf, coordinator of the Arab group.
Lebanese Foreign Minister Faris Bouez said on leaving Beirut he wanted the 27 ministers to call for resumed Middle East peace talks under the guidelines set at the Madrid conference in 1991.

The key concepts in Madrid were "land for peace" -- rejected by Netanyahu -- and a ban on unilateral steps which prejudice the outcome of talks on the final status of Jerusalem and the occupied territories.
The Europeans do not disagree with Bouez but, like the United States, are seeking a practical way out of the impasse.
A spokesman for the European Union's special Middle East envoy, Miguel Angel Moratinos, said last week the Europeans had prepared an initiative with this aim.

It calls on both parties to abstain from unilateral actions, for Israel to freeze Jewish settlement on occupied land and for Palestinians to make a stronger commitment to prevent political violence, he said.
But the initiative appears to please neither side and the Europeans have not been saying much more about it in public.
Netanyahu says he will never renounce an Israeli "right" to settle Jews in East Jerusalem and the West Bank.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said on Saturday the European initiative was better than what the United States had to offer but still was not up to Arab expectations.
